children.prompt: Find the area bounded by $y=x^2-x-2$, the $x$-axis, and lines $x=-2$ and $x=1$.

spec.description: Equation-driven upward-opening parabola, double-ended axes, curve-end arrowheads and no ticks. Light green shading identifies the requested area; green vertical boundaries mark the interval endpoints.
spec.mathematics: y=x^2-x-2, roots -1 and 2; shaded interval [-2,1], with a positive region on [-2,-1] and a negative region on [-1,1].
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied curve and shaded region appear; no calculated roots, values or answers are labelled.

answer.worked:
Find the $x$-intercepts.
$$\begin{align*}
x^2-x-2&=0\\
(x-2)(x+1)&=0\\
x&=-1,\ 2
\end{align*}$$
Only $x=-1$ lies inside the interval $[-2,1]$.
$$\begin{align*}
A&=\int_{-2}^{-1}(x^2-x-2)\,dx+\left|\int_{-1}^{1}(x^2-x-2)\,dx\right|\\
A&=\left[\frac{x^3}{3}-\frac{x^2}{2}-2x\right]_{-2}^{-1}+\left|\left[\frac{x^3}{3}-\frac{x^2}{2}-2x\right]_{-1}^{1}\right|\\
A&=\left(\frac76-\left(-\frac23\right)\right)+\left| -\frac{13}{6}-\frac76\right|\\
A&=\frac{11}{6}+\left|-\frac{10}{3}\right|\\
A&=\frac{31}{6}\text{ units}^2
\end{align*}$$

spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens and shaded regions appear; roots and calculated areas are not labelled.

answer.worked:
Find the $x$-intercepts.
$$\begin{align*}
x(x+1)(x-2)&=0\\
x&=-1,\ 0,\ 2
\end{align*}$$
Split the enclosed area at $x=0$.
$$\begin{align*}
x(x+1)(x-2)&=x^3-x^2-2x\\
A&=\int_{-1}^{0}(x^3-x^2-2x)\,dx+\left|\int_{0}^{2}(x^3-x^2-2x)\,dx\right|\\
A&=\left[\frac{x^4}{4}-\frac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_{-1}^{0}+\left|\left[\frac{x^4}{4}-\frac{x^3}{3}-x^2\right]_{0}^{2}\right|\\
A&=0-\left(\frac14+\frac13-1\right)+\left|4-\frac83-4-0\right|\\
A&=\frac5{12}+\left|-\frac83\right|\\
A&=\frac{37}{12}\text{ units}^2
\end{align*}$$

answer.short: $\dfrac52$. The integral gives the area above the $x$-axis minus the area below it, rather than the total area.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\int_{-3}^{2}(x+1)\,dx&=\left[\frac{x^2}{2}+x\right]_{-3}^{2}\\&=(2+2)-\left(\frac92-3\right)\\&=\frac52.\end{align*}$$

The zero is $x=3$. The curve is below the $x$-axis on $[-1,3]$ and above it on $[3,4]$.
$$\begin{aligned}A_{\text{below}}&=-\int_{-1}^{3}(x-3)\,dx\\&=-\left[\frac{x^2}{2}-3x\right]_{-1}^{3}\\&=-\left[\left(\frac92-9\right)-\left(\frac12+3\right)\right]\\&=8.\end{aligned}$$

$$A=8+\frac12=8\frac12\text{ units}^2.$$

$y=x^3-7x+6$, with zeros at $x=-3,1,2$.
On $(-3,1)$, checking $x=0$ gives $y=6>0$, so the curve is above the $x$-axis. On $(1,2)$, checking $x=1.5$ gives $y=-1.125<0$, so it is below.
$$F(x)=\frac{x^4}{4}-\frac{7x^2}{2}+6x.$$

$y=-2x(x+1)=-2x^2-2x$, with zeros at $x=-1$ and $x=0$.

answer.worked:
$y=x^7$ is odd, so the areas on $[-2,0]$ and $[0,2]$ are equal. On $[0,2]$, the curve is above the $x$-axis.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=2\int_0^2x^7\,dx\\&=2\left[\frac{x^8}{8}\right]_0^2\\&=2\left(\frac{256}{8}-0\right)\\&=64\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

The function is odd, so its graph is symmetric about the origin. Its zeros are $x=-4,0,4$.
On $[0,4]$, $x(x-4)(x+4)\le0$. For example, at $x=2$, $y=2(-2)(6)=-24$, below the $x$-axis.
By symmetry,
$$A=2\left(-\int_0^4(x^3-16x)\,dx\right).$$
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^4(x^3-16x)\,dx&=\left[\frac{x^4}{4}-8x^2\right]_0^4\\&=(64-128)-0\\&=-64\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}A&=2(64)\\&=128\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

The function is even, so its graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis. Its zeros are $x=-3,0,3$.
On $[0,3]$, the curve is on or below the $x$-axis. For example, at $x=1$, $y=1-9=-8$.
By symmetry,
$$A=2\left(-\int_0^3(x^4-9x^2)\,dx\right).$$
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^3(x^4-9x^2)\,dx&=\left[\frac{x^5}{5}-3x^3\right]_0^3\\&=\left(\frac{243}{5}-81\right)-0\\&=-\frac{162}{5}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}A&=2\left(\frac{162}{5}\right)\\&=\frac{324}{5}\\&=64\frac45\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

answer.short: $\dfrac{\pi}{8}$. The right-endpoint Riemann sum is four times the given sum and tends to the semicircle area $\pi/2$ for all positive integers $n$.
answer.worked:
Let $S_n=\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{\sqrt{r(n-r)}}{n^2}$. The term with $r=n$ is zero.
For even $n$, parts (b) and (c) give
$$4S_n-\frac{2}{n}\leq\frac{\pi}{2}\leq4S_n+\frac{2}{n}.$$
Thus $S_n\to\pi/8$ along the even positive integers.
To establish the limit for all positive integers $n$, use the limit of rectangle sums. The function $f(x)=\sqrt{x(2-x)}$ is continuous on $[0,2]$. For the equal partition with width $2/n$, the right-endpoint rectangle sum is
$$\begin{align*}
R_n&=\frac{2}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n}f\left(\frac{2r}{n}\right)\\
&=\frac{2}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n}\sqrt{\frac{2r}{n}\left(2-\frac{2r}{n}\right)}\\
&=4\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{\sqrt{r(n-r)}}{n^2}\\
&=4S_n.
\end{align*}$$
As $n\to\infty$ through all positive integers, the rectangle width tends to zero, so the Riemann sums tend to the definite integral:
$$\begin{align*}
\lim_{n\to\infty}R_n&=\int_0^2f(x)\,dx=\frac{\pi}{2},\\
\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n&=\frac14\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}=\frac{\pi}{8}.
\end{align*}$$
